name: Jamal Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and fit raised timber floors on building sites, now in a data-centre equipment hall. A vocational trade certificate got me started and difficult cable rooms pay me above the standard rate, though I am an experienced fitter rather than the foreman. I like a level finished floor; carrying panels around live cables makes me slow down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in bookkeeping and our children are grown. We have nine months of expenses saved and many similar builders nearby. I use AI daily for panel cut lists, but measure each cable hatch myself; I hope to finish regular site work around 67 if our retirement income and my knees allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the raised-floor crew AI can count panels faster, and I already use it each morning. The machine still doesn't feel a loose pedestal under the deck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn more than a standard carpenter because I fit difficult equipment-room floors, and my partner's bookkeeping work is steady. We have nine months of expenses saved, grown children and many builders nearby, so this mild picture leaves retirement in sight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting the data-centre floor panels and use my daily AI cut list, checking it against the actual cable openings. My partner and I will review our retirement income this year; I hope to finish regular site work around 67 if the figures support it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little pleasure in having fewer panel counts to redo. I don't need to call a modest tool a revolution to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the AI cut list miss a floor detail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cut list put a solid panel over a cable hatch last week. I changed the order before the floor was sealed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your retirement review decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The retirement check will compare both income statements with our spending, including repairs on our home. It tells us whether 67 is affordable; it is not a notice that I'm leaving work now.

say: **AI panel counts** save time, but cable openings still need a site check.
The **raised floor** remains hands-on work with physical safety checks.
think: My **higher site wage** and partner's income keep the present secure.
Nine months of **expenses saved** and many local builders make planning easier.
do: **Fit** data-centre raised floor and check AI cut lists against cable hatches.
**Compare** retirement income statements with household spending this year.
feel: **Calm** about work and money, curious about useful AI.
S0.quote: The cut list put a solid panel over a cable hatch last week.
fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** for cutting lists but catches a cable-access error through a site check.
His hoped-for exit at **67 is conditional** on current income statements, not a decision to stop work now.

steps.text: Fit data-centre floor and check daily AI lists against cable hatches
Compare retirement income statements with household spending this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI can do more buying and booking while the robots take longer to place floor panels around live cables. I would ask the contractor to show us the new plan before the truck arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own installation shifts look secure and we have savings and other builders nearby. The office may waste a day with a bad panel order, but I can learn the new editor and correct it before anyone loses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll try the updated AI floor-layout editor on an unused equipment room and learn its cable-hatch controls. I'll compare the cut list with the measured room, then show the crew and the site buyer which edits saved a return trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my income and interested in a useful new screen. A fair test on a quiet room is easier than an argument after the panels arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you mark before ordering panels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark each cable hatch on the measured floor drawing before ordering the panels. A tidy digital grid is no use if the technician cannot reach a cable underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the new editor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count actual panels cut twice and the time spent correcting the list. If the editor adds errors, we keep the measured drawing as the order until it improves.

say: **AI buying and booking** expand before robots can place raised floors.
Workers should see **measured cable openings** before orders are sent.
think: My **installation wage** looks secure with local alternatives and savings.
A wrong **panel order** could waste time, but I can test a correction early.
do: **Learn** updated AI floor-layout controls in an unused equipment room.
**Compare** new cut list with measured cable hatches before ordering.
feel: **Calm** about income, interested in a controlled tool test.
S1.quote: A tidy digital grid is no use if the technician cannot reach a cable underneath.
fieldNote: He takes **new AI learning** onto an unused room, measuring duplicate cuts and correction time before live use.
His wage stays **secure now** in the slower change, supported by strong savings and plentiful nearby builders.

steps.text: Learn updated AI floor-layout controls in unused equipment room
Compare new panel list with measured cable hatches before ordering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 may design and order the floors, then capable robots around 2031 could fit them. The contractor should put paid crew numbers and a safe trial plan in front of the fitters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 63 when robots can do physical installation, four years before my hoped-for exit at 67. Nine months saved and plenty of local builders are a bridge, but a cut to my higher-paid shifts could still leave a gap in our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the site worker committee for a meeting on robot exclusion zones and paid trial roles. If the contractor offers a funded, recognised floor-inspection course with a real place and full wages on class days, I'll enrol; if it cuts my shifts first, I'll apply only to posted local fit-out jobs with safe duties and pay that covers our household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible income gap at 63, though I can move early and our reserve buys time. I would rather learn a real skill than watch a robot demonstration from the back row.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe robot floor trial require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test a robot on a floor with a real cable hatch, an exclusion zone and a fitter able to stop it. A robot fitting a showroom panel would not show what happens beside electricians' tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a course or job real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course must have fees paid, a place, normal class wages and an assessment on a real floor. A new job must be posted locally with hours I can do safely and pay sufficient for our bills.

say: **2028 thinking AI** designs floors before robots install panels around 2031.
Workers need **paid crew figures** and safe robot trials.
think: At about **63**, robot fitters could cut my higher-paid shifts before I hope to leave at 67.
Nine months of **savings** and local builders help, but cannot replace four years of wages.
do: **Ask** site worker committee for safe paid robot trial meeting.
**Enrol** in funded recognised floor-inspection course if real place and full class wages offered.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local fit-out job with safe duties and bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost income before affordable retirement.
S2.quote: A robot fitting a showroom panel would not show what happens beside electricians' tools.
fieldNote: He uses a **worker committee** to demand paid trials, exclusion zones and a fitter with stop authority.
Course and job conditions include **funding and class wages**, a real place, posted local work, safe duties and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Ask worker committee for paid robot trial and safety meeting
Enrol in funded recognised floor-inspection course if real place and full class wages offered
Apply after cuts to posted local fit-out job with safe duties and bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2031 could make floor layouts, then robots around 2034 could set the panels. Five years is enough to train a site checker and learn what the machine does beside a cable hatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 66 when robots can fit the floor, roughly a year before I hope to stop if our income permits. If the contractor cuts the high-paid shifts then, nine months of savings would help, but I may still need a year's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll attend the free evening site-equipment safety introduction this winter while keeping my fitting shifts. If the contractor funds a recognised inspection certificate with a real place and paid assessment leave, I'll enrol next year; after qualifying, if my shifts are cut and retirement income is short, I'll apply only to posted local equipment-checking jobs with safe hours and pay covering our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible final-year pay gap, but keen to use the warning time. The free class is a start, not a promised inspection post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should hands-on training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the trainer stop the machine when a panel edge sits over a hatch. I want to work a site robot's stop control myself, not just see a green light on its screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to take another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare our actual retirement statements with bills before taking a different post. A high-sounding title with lower pay or unsafe lifting would not solve the gap.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes layouts before robots place floor panels around 2034.
Five years allows **hands-on safety training** at real cable hatches.
think: At about **66**, one year of higher wages may still be needed.
Nine months of **savings** will not automatically close a retirement shortfall.
do: **Attend** free evening site-equipment safety introduction while still employed.
**Enrol** in recognised inspection certificate if funded place and paid assessment leave secured.
**Apply** after qualification and cuts if income short to posted local job with safe bill-covering hours.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible last-year wage gap, with a training plan.
S3.quote: I want to work a site robot's stop control myself, not just see a green light on its screen.
fieldNote: He starts **actual free study** and requires a funded recognised place with paid assessment time before further enrolment.
The application needs **qualification and cuts**, then an income shortfall and posted local work with safe bill-covering hours.

steps.text: Attend free evening site-equipment safety introduction while employed
Enrol in recognised inspection certificate if funded place and paid leave secured
Apply after qualification and cuts if income short to posted local job with safe bill-covering hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 may draw floor layouts and robots around 2039 may fit panels. I hope to be off regular sites by 67 if our income works, and the younger crew should have proper paid time to learn safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 71 when robots can do the hands-on fitting, beyond my hoped-for exit. Our current statements and nine-month reserve suggest a workable plan, but my partner and I will still check real income each year before treating 67 as settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting floors and checking hatch access on the current site rota. At the worker committee's next meeting I'll propose paid apprenticeships for floor safety checks; my partner and I will review retirement statements annually, and if the figures support leaving around 67, I'll hand the hatch notes to a younger fitter before I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our near-term money and the long time to plan. I can enjoy teaching the next worker without claiming I will still be installing floors in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a younger floor fitter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the younger fitter where a panel can cover the only route to a cable joint. A floor robot's neat grid does not tell an electrician where to lift safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the committee proposal work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The committee proposal would name paid apprentice hours, a real floor section and a fitter who signs the hatch check. I would take our current inspection sheet to the meeting.

say: **2036 thinking AI** plans floors before robots install panels around 2039.
**Paid hatch checks** should be taught before experienced fitters leave.
think: At about **71**, robots likely arrive after my hoped-for exit at 67.
Actual **retirement statements** still decide whether that exit is affordable.
do: **Keep** fitting floors and checking cable hatches on current rota.
**Propose** paid floor-safety apprenticeship at worker committee meeting.
**Review** retirement statements with partner annually before conditional handover.
feel: **Calm** about current money, interested in a paid handover.
S4.quote: A floor robot's neat grid does not tell an electrician where to lift safely.
fieldNote: He separates **current paid work** from a conditional handover before retirement, without asserting site work at 71.
The **worker committee** gives his paid apprentice proposal a concrete group setting and safety checklist.

steps.text: Keep fitting floors and checking cable hatches on current rota

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because floor robots around 2031 could cut high-paid shifts at about 63, before our planned income may support leaving work. A paid safety trial, funded course and actual posted local jobs with safe duties and adequate pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the cable hatch after a robot closes the raised floor. A floor can be level and still lock the electrician out of the cable joint. I want the access check signed before handover.

headlineQuote: A floor can be level and still lock the electrician out of the cable joint.
portrait: **Jamal**, 58, fits raised floors on building sites with a vocational certificate and higher pay from difficult cable rooms.
His bookkeeper partner and grown children share a **nine-month reserve**, with plentiful nearby construction jobs.
He uses **AI daily** for panel lists, learns new controls early and brings safety training proposals to a worker committee.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about wages before a conditional exit around 67; a decade supports a paid handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring floor robots around 2031 when he would be about 63 and might still need wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid safety trial**, funded inspection course and real posted local roles with safe duties and adequate pay would help.
